claim: SABRE is found throughout eukaryotes and was originally identified in plants
source: SABRE, which is found throughout eukaryotes and was originally identified in plants, mediates cell expansion, division plane orientation, and planar polarity in plants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about SABRE

claim: SABRE mediates cell expansion, division plane orientation, and planar polarity in plants
source: SABRE, which is found throughout eukaryotes and was originally identified in plants, mediates cell expansion, division plane orientation, and planar polarity in plants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about SABRE function

claim: SABRE null mutants in Physcomitrium patens are stunted
source: SABRE null mutants were stunted, similar to phenotypes in seed plants.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1

claim: SABRE null mutant phenotypes in moss are similar to phenotypes in seed plants
source: SABRE null mutants were stunted, similar to phenotypes in seed plants.
evidence: This comparison is explicitly stated in the abstract

claim: Polarized growing cells in SABRE null mutants are delayed in cytokinesis
source: Additionally, polarized growing cells were delayed in cytokinesis, sometimes resulting in catastrophic failures.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3

claim: Cytokinesis delays in SABRE null mutants sometimes result in catastrophic failures
source: Additionally, polarized growing cells were delayed in cytokinesis, sometimes resulting in catastrophic failures.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3

claim: A functional SABRE fluorescent fusion protein localizes to dynamic puncta on regions of the endoplasmic reticulum during interphase
source: A functional SABRE fluorescent fusion protein localized to dynamic puncta on regions of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) during interphase and at the cell plate during cell division.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5

claim: A functional SABRE fluorescent fusion protein localizes at the cell plate during cell division
source: A functional SABRE fluorescent fusion protein localized to dynamic puncta on regions of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) during interphase and at the cell plate during cell division.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Cells lacking SABRE accumulate ER aggregates
source: Without SABRE, cells accumulated ER aggregates and the ER abnormally buckled along the developing cell plate.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6

claim: The ER abnormally buckles along the developing cell plate in cells lacking SABRE
source: Without SABRE, cells accumulated ER aggregates and the ER abnormally buckled along the developing cell plate.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6

claim: Callose deposition is delayed in ∆sabre mutants
source: Notably, callose deposition was delayed in ∆sabre, and in cells that failed to divide, abnormal callose accumulations formed at the cell plate.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 8

claim: Abnormal callose accumulations form at the cell plate in ∆sabre cells that fail to divide
source: Notably, callose deposition was delayed in ∆sabre, and in cells that failed to divide, abnormal callose accumulations formed at the cell plate.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 8

claim: The ER plays a fundamental role in cell plate maturation
source: Our findings revealed a surprising and fundamental role for the ER in cell plate maturation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract based on the findings

claim: Plants regulate growth patterns by adjusting to their environment due to their sessile nature
source: Due to their sessile nature, plants cannot simply run away from environmental stimuli and instead must adjust to their environment by regulating growth patterns.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction

claim: Plant growth involves deposition of extracellular matrix material (the cell wall) around individual cells and cell expansion
source: Plant growth is a coupled process involving deposition of extracellular matrix material – the cell wall – around individual cells and cell expansion.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction

claim: Precise regulation of cell wall composition determines where a particular cell can expand
source: Precise regulation of the composition of this matrix ensures where a particular cell can expand.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction

claim: Polarity cues at cellular and tissue levels ensure coordination that patterns whole organs in plants
source: To control cell shape throughout a tissue, polarity cues at the cellular and tissue level ensure coordination ultimately patterning whole organs, such as correctly oriented roots and stems (Blilou et al., 2005; Kania et al., 2014; van Dop et al., 2020), as well as specialized structures including stomata and root hairs (Gilroy and Jones, 2000; Houbaert et al., 2018; Mansfield et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

claim: Cell division plane positioning contributes to cell shape and provides polarity information
source: Positioning the cell division plane contributes to cell shape and provides polarity information (Zhang and Dong, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: In root and shoot tissue in seed plants, the cell division plane is perpendicular to the growth axis
source: For example, in root and shoot tissue in seed plants, the cell division plane is perpendicular to the growth axis and creates polygonal cells that are aligned longitudinally with each other (Ambrose et al., 2007; Galjart, 2005; Schaefer et al., 2017; Smith et al., 1996; Walker et al., 2007), ensuring that expansion is aligned uniformly with the overall plant growth axis.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

claim: The sabre mutant was first identified in Arabidopsis in the early 1990s
source: The sabre mutant, which has short fat roots, was first identified in Arabidopsis in the early 1990s (Benfey et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: The sabre mutant has short fat roots
source: The sabre mutant, which has short fat roots, was first identified in Arabidopsis in the early 1990s (Benfey et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Increased root diameter in sabre mutants results from exaggerated radial expansion primarily in root cortex cells
source: The increased root diameter resulted from exaggerated radial expansion primarily in root cortex cells, suggesting that SABRE plays a role in regulating expansion of diffusely growing cells (Aeschbacher et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: KINKY POLLEN (KIP) is a second copy of SABRE in Arabidopsis
source: A second copy of SABRE, named KINKY POLLEN (KIP), which is expressed most strongly in roots, pollen, and developing seeds, was identified in a screen for abnormal pollen tube and root hair morphology (Procissi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: KIP is expressed most strongly in roots, pollen, and developing seeds
source: A second copy of SABRE, named KINKY POLLEN (KIP), which is expressed most strongly in roots, pollen, and developing seeds, was identified in a screen for abnormal pollen tube and root hair morphology (Procissi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Plants lacking KIP form defective pollen tubes that exhibit periods of relatively normal growth interspersed with periods of slow or arrested growth
source: Plants lacking KIP form defective pollen tubes that exhibit periods of relatively normal growth interspersed with periods of slow or arrested growth.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Root hairs are shorter and thicker in kip mutants
source: In addition, root hairs were shorter and thicker in kip mutants (Procissi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: The homozygous kip/sab double mutant exhibits enhanced phenotypes in both diffuse and polarized growing tissues
source: However, the homozygous kip/sab double mutant exhibited enhanced phenotypes in both diffuse and polarized growing tissues, indicating overlapping function of these two closely related genes (Procissi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Cell plate positioning in the root meristem is variable in sabre mutants
source: More recent studies have found that in sabre mutants cell plate positioning in the root meristem was variable, resulting in cells that were not cylindrically aligned.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Root hair emergence is no longer restricted to the basal portion of the trichoblast cell in sabre mutants
source: Furthermore, root hair emergence was no longer restricted to the basal portion of the trichoblast cell (Pietra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Physcomitrium patens is an excellent cell biological model system for studying how cell shape affects developmental patterning
source: Among plants, the moss Physcomitrium (formerly Physcomitrella) patens is an excellent cell biological model system and ideal for studying how cell shape affects developmental patterning (Rensing et al., 2020; Rounds and Bezanilla, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

claim: Moss juvenile tissue (protonemata) is haploid and comprises a filamentous two-dimensional branching network that is a single-cell layer thick
source: Moss juvenile tissue, protonemata, is haploid and comprises a filamentous two-dimensional branching network that is a single-cell layer thick, making it readily amenable to high-resolution microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the model system

claim: P. patens has a single copy of SABRE
source: Furthermore, in contrast to seed plants, P. patens has a single copy of SABRE and plants can be propagated asexually, avoiding potential problems resulting from defects in sexual reproduction.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the model system

claim: The P. patens genome has one SABRE gene that encodes for a 2736 aa protein
source: The P. patens genome has one SABRE gene that encodes for a 2736 aa protein.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from genomic analysis

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair was used to insert a 363 bp cassette with stop codons in all three possible frames into exon 2 of the SABRE locus
source: To disrupt SABRE, we used CRISPR-Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair (HDR) to insert a 363 bp cassette with stop codons in all three possible frames into exon 2 of the SABRE locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The mutant allele results in a frame shift starting at amino acid 38 followed by a premature stop codon after amino acid 47
source: The mutant allele results in a frame shift starting at amino acid 38 followed by a premature stop codon after amino acid 47.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the genetic modification

claim: ∆sabre plants have smaller and more compact protonemata compared to wild type
source: Compared to wild type, ∆sabre plants had smaller and more compact protonemata (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Figure 1A

claim: ∆sabre protonemata are 60% smaller than control plants
source: Compared to protonemata in control plants, we found that ∆sabre protonemata were 60% smaller (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 1C

claim: ∆sabre gametophores are 36% shorter than wild type
source: We also observed that ∆sabre gametophores are 36% shorter than wild type (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 1D and E

claim: ∆sabre phyllids are 22% smaller than wild type
source: The phyllids, leaf-like structures that emanate from the gametophore, were 22% smaller than wild type (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 1F

claim: ∆sabre rhizoids are 70% shorter than wild type rhizoids
source: ∆sabre rhizoids were 70% shorter than wild type rhizoids, a decrease in size comparable to the polarized-growing protonemata (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 1G

claim: Early developmental patterning of ∆sabre gametophores is not altered
source: Time-lapse imaging demonstrated that while early developmental patterning of ∆sabre gametophores was not altered, cell expansion was significantly delayed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1

claim: Cell expansion is significantly delayed in ∆sabre gametophores
source: Time-lapse imaging demonstrated that while early developmental patterning of ∆sabre gametophores was not altered, cell expansion was significantly delayed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1

claim: The single SABRE gene regulates both polarized and diffuse growth in P. patens
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the single SABRE gene regulates both polarized and diffuse growth in P. patens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 1

claim: ∆sabre protonemal subapical cells are 30% shorter than wild type
source: While ∆sabre cells were 30% shorter than wild type (Figure 2A), the decrease of overall plant size was 60% (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 2A

claim: Actively growing ∆sabre cells grow only 20% slower than control cells on average
source: While on average actively growing ∆sabre cells grew only 20% slower than control cells, the reduction in growth was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from time-lapse imaging

claim: ∆sabre protonemal filaments often grow significantly less than wild type due to frequent long pauses in growth
source: In contrast, time-lapse imaging revealed that over the same time period ∆sabre protonemal filaments often grew significantly less than a comparable wild type filament due to the fact that for a large portion of the time-lapse acquisition the ∆sabre cell was not growing (Figure 2B, Video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 2B and Video 2

claim: ∆sabre protonemata often change direction during growth
source: Interestingly, ∆sabre protonemal cells often changed direction during growth (Figure 2B, Video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 2B and Video 2

claim: The actin and microtubule foci in ∆sabre cells are persistently present at the tip similar to wild type
source: We found that similar to wild type, the actin and microtubule foci in ∆sabre cells were persistently present at the tip (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Defects in growth directionality and rate in ∆sabre appear to be independent of actin and microtubules
source: Thus, the observed defects in growth directionality and rate appear to be independent of actin and microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cytoskeleton imaging data

claim: Cortical actin exhibits a slight increase in dynamics in ∆sabre
source: However, cortical actin exhibited a slight increase in dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from VAEM imaging supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Cell area at the base and tip of phyllids is reduced in ∆sabre
source: We quantified cell size in fully expanded phyllids and discovered that cell area at the base and tip of phyllids was reduced in ∆sabre (Figure 2D–F), consistent with the overall stunted gametophore stature (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 2D-F

claim: Cell area at the base of phyllids is more affected than cells at the tip of the phyllid in ∆sabre
source: In particular, cell area at the base of phyllids, which are generally the largest cells in the phyllid, was more affected than cells at the tip of the phyllid in ∆sabre (Figure 2E), suggesting that in the absence of SABRE cells may not be able to expand beyond a certain size.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 2E with an interpretation

claim: Cells are less elongated in ∆sabre both at the tip and the base of the phyllids compared to wild type
source: Cells were less elongated in ∆sabre both at the tip and the base of the phyllids compared to wild type (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by Figure 2F

claim: Mitosis is unaltered in ∆sabre protonemata
source: In ∆sabre protonemata, we discovered that while mitosis is unaltered (e.g., Figure 3A, 0–12 min), phragmoplast microtubules were present for significantly longer than in control cells (Figure 3A, Video 4).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 3A and Video 4

claim: Phragmoplast microtubules are present for significantly longer in ∆sabre cells than in control cells
source: In ∆sabre protonemata, we discovered that while mitosis is unaltered (e.g., Figure 3A, 0–12 min), phragmoplast microtubules were present for significantly longer than in control cells (Figure 3A, Video 4).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 3A and Video 4

claim: All control cell phragmoplast microtubules disappear within 28–50 min after disc phragmoplast establishment
source: We found that starting at the time of disc phragmoplast establishment (Figure 3A, 12 min), all control cell phragmoplast microtubules disappeared within 28–50 min (N = 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 3A

claim: For all ∆sabre cells, microtubules are still present for at least 50 min after disc phragmoplast establishment
source: However, for all ∆sabre cells (N = 10), microtubules were still present for at least 50 min after disc phragmoplast establishment.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from time-lapse imaging

claim: Microtubule fluorescence recovers from photobleaching similarly in control and ∆sabre cells
source: Microtubule fluorescence recovered from photobleaching similarly in control and ∆sabre cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that SABRE does not regulate microtubule dynamics during phragmoplast expansion.
evidence: This is a finding from photobleaching experiments supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: SABRE does not regulate microtubule dynamics during phragmoplast expansion
source: Microtubule fluorescence recovered from photobleaching similarly in control and ∆sabre cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that SABRE does not regulate microtubule dynamics during phragmoplast expansion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from photobleaching experiments

claim: A fraction of ∆sabre cells contain dark brown material that accumulates near the cell division plane
source: Besides the lengthy delay in phragmoplast microtubule disassembly in protonemata, we observed that a fraction of cells contained dark brown material, which accumulated near the cell division plane (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy supported by Figure 3B-D

claim: Brown material deposition in ∆sabre cells is slow and always initiates during a cell division event
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that brown material deposition was slow (Figure 3D, Figure 3, Video 5), but always initiated during a cell division event.
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 3D and Video 5

claim: Cells with brown material either reinitiate growth after a long recovery time or die
source: Cells with brown material would either reinitiate growth after a long recovery time or die (Figure 3, Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Video 5

claim: Brown material appears more frequently in cells with a large diameter in ∆sabre
source: Interestingly, brown material appeared more frequently in cells with a large diameter, characteristic of the first few cells in plants regenerated from protoplasts (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy supported by Figure 3B and C

claim: ∆sabre protoplasts regenerate inefficiently compared to wild type
source: We also noticed that ∆sabre protoplasts regenerated inefficiently compared to wild type, likely because many protoplasts died during the first cell division, with brown material deposited at the cell division site (Figure 3B, yellow arrow).
evidence: This is a finding from protoplast regeneration experiments supported by Figure 3B

claim: Tagging SABRE at its C terminus with three tandem mEGFPs or mNeonGreens does not influence its function
source: We demonstrated that tagging SABRE at its C terminus with either three tandem mEGFPs (Vidali et al., 2009)﻿ or mNeonGreens did not influence its function as we observed no growth defects in plants carrying only the tagged SABRE allele (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from functional complementation experiments supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: SAB-3mNG forms small puncta at the cell cortex with highest density near the tip of the apical cell
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that SAB-3mNG formed small puncta at the cell cortex, whose density was highest near the tip of the apical cell (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from confocal microscopy supported by Figure 4A

claim: OE-SAB-3mNG plants are indistinguishable from SAB-3mNG plants
source: Importantly, OE-SAB-3mNG plants were indistinguishable from SAB-3mNG plants, demonstrating that overexpression did not have any adverse consequences for protonemal growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: OE-SAB-3mNG forms discrete puncta decorating the entire developing cell plate during cell division
source: During cell division, OE-SAB-3mNG formed discrete puncta decorating the entire developing cell plate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from confocal microscopy supported by Figure 4B

claim: Cortical SABRE puncta do not associate with microtubules
source: Consistent with the finding that microtubules were not affected in ∆sabre plants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, C) and that SABRE localizes to the nascent cell plate even in late phragmoplasts that lack microtubules (Figure 4B), we found that cortical SABRE puncta did not associate with microtubules (Figure 4C, Figure 4, Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding from VAEM imaging supported by Figure 4C and Video 6

claim: Limited overlap exists between SABRE and actin at the cell cortex
source: We observed limited overlap between SABRE and actin at the cell cortex (Figure 4C, Figure 4, Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding from VAEM imaging supported by Figure 4C and Video 6

claim: Cortical SABRE dynamically associates with ER tubules
source: However, most surprisingly, we discovered that cortical SABRE dynamically associated with ER tubules (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B,, Video 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding from VAEM imaging supported by Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B, and Video 6

claim: On average 57% of SABRE puncta area overlaps with cortical ER tubules
source: Using this method, we found that on average 57% of SABRE puncta area overlapped with cortical ER tubules (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from image analysis supported by Figure 4E

claim: Overexpression of SABRE does not significantly affect ER overlap
source: However, importantly overexpression did not significantly affect the ER overlap (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from image analysis supported by Figure 4E

claim: OE-SAB-3mNG localizes to the midzone of the ring phragmoplast weakly, and the signal strengthens as the phragmoplast fully expands and inserts into the side wall
source: Confocal time-lapse imaging revealed that OE-SAB-3mNG localized to the midzone of the ring phragmoplast weakly, and the signal strengthened as the phragmoplast fully expanded and inserted into the side wall (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from confocal time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The strongest OE-SAB-3mNG signal correlates with the timing of cell plate maturation
source: The strongest OE-SAB-3mNG signal correlated with the timing of cell plate maturation (Figure 5A, B, Video 7) and remained until the ER signal visibly split in two on either side of the new cell plate (last two time points of Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from confocal time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 5A, B, and Video 7

claim: ∆sabre cells contain abnormal ER aggregates in the cytoplasm in protonemata
source: We discovered that ∆sabre cells contained abnormal ER aggregates in the cytoplasm in protonemata, which might underlie defects in polarized growth and directionality (Figure 6A, Video 8).
evidence: This is a finding from ER imaging supported by Figure 6A and Video 8

claim: The cell plate ER signal noticeably buckles in ∆sabre during cell division
source: However, during the transition to an increase in ER parallel to the cell plate, the cell plate ER signal noticeably buckled in ∆sabre, while in control cells the ER was straight (Figure 6B, magenta arrowheads, Video 9).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 6B and Video 9

claim: Buckling in ∆sabre mutants occurs coincident with the timing of maximal SABRE accumulation on the cell plate in control cells
source: Interestingly buckling in ∆sabre mutants occurred coincident with the timing of maximal SABRE accumulation on the cell plate in control cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a temporal correlation observed between Figures 5 and 6

claim: Phragmoplast guidance mechanisms and the phragmoplast insertion site are not affected in ∆sabre
source: Note that while twisting of the ER was obvious in the center of the cell plate, the edges adjacent to the side wall remained fixed, indicating that phragmoplast guidance mechanisms and the phragmoplast insertion site were not affected (Figure 6B, Figure 6, Video 9).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from ER imaging supported by Figure 6B and Video 9

claim: The twisted ER in ∆sabre cells that divide relatively normally eventually straightens out 20–30 min later
source: For ∆sabre cells that divided relatively normally, the twisted ER, which was observed in all ∆sabre cells (N = 31), eventually straightened out 20–30 min later (Figure 6B, Figure 6, Video 9).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 6B and Video 9

claim: Nuclei in ∆sabre apical cells exhibit aberrant motility during cell division
source: In addition to ER buckling, we noticed that nuclei in ∆sabre apical cells exhibited aberrant motility during cell division.
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging

claim: The initial apical movement of the nucleus is delayed in 39% of ∆sabre cells
source: In ∆sabre cells, the initial apical movement of the nucleus was delayed in 39% of the 31 imaged cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, green arrowheads, Video 10), resulting in a close association between the nucleus and the cell plate, and coinciding with ER buckling (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, magenta arrowheads, Video 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Video 10

claim: The basal nuclear movement is dramatically exaggerated in all ∆sabre cells
source: While the phase I apical nuclear movement was normal in the remaining 61% of imaged ∆sabre cells, the subsequent basal movement was dramatically exaggerated in all cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, red arrowheads, Video 10).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Video 10

claim: The relative basal nuclear position is significantly smaller in ∆sabre than in control cells
source: To quantify the defect in basal movement, we measured the distance between the nucleus and the cell plate when the nucleus was closest to the cell plate (basal position), normalizing the basal position to the apical cell length at that time point. Despite shorter cells in ∆sabre, the relative basal nuclear position was significantly smaller than in control cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from nuclear tracking supported by Figure 6D

claim: ∆sabre nuclear movement is less linear than wild type
source: We discovered that ∆sabre nuclear movement was less linear and the ratio was smaller (Figure 6E) compared to wild type.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from nuclear tracking supported by Figure 6E

claim: The average instantaneous velocity of the nucleus in ∆sabre is smaller than wild type
source: The average instantaneous velocity of the nucleus in ∆sabre was expectedly smaller since the cells were not always actively growing (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from nuclear tracking supported by Figure 6F

claim: Defects in nuclear migration in ∆sabre likely result from altered ER function
source: Given that SABRE influences the ER and that the nuclear envelope is contiguous with the ER, defects in nuclear migration likely result from altered ER function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ER and nuclear migration data

claim: The ER signal transitions from defined tubules to a diffuse signal in ∆sabre cells that fail to form a normal cell plate
source: We observed the ER signal transition from defined tubules (Figure 7A, 40 min) in the phragmoplast to a diffuse signal (Figure 7A, 50 min), correlating with the onset of division failure.
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 7A

claim: Brown material is outlined by the ER signal in ∆sabre cells that fail to divide
source: As the brown material accumulated, it was outlined by the ER signal (Figure 7A, Figure 7, Video 12).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse imaging supported by Figure 7A and Video 12

claim: Phragmoplast expansion is normal in ∆sabre
source: Taken together our data suggest that phragmoplast expansion is normal in ∆sabre.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cytoskeleton imaging data in Figure 7

claim: During cell plate maturation, defects arise in ∆sabre cells where the ER becomes diffuse and both the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons remain associated with the cell plate
source: However, during cell plate maturation, defects arise in ∆sabre cells; the ER becomes diffuse and both the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons remain associated with the cell plate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data in Figure 7

claim: SABRE plays a role in cell plate maturation influencing the timing of callose deposition
source: Our data demonstrate that SABRE plays a role in cell plate maturation influencing the timing of callose deposition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the callose staining data

claim: ∆sabre cells exhibit unregulated callose deposition and remodeling
source: For ∆sabre cells that accumulated brown material, we observed a range of different callose staining behavior and time-lapse imaging revealed that large callose aggregates were not static, suggesting that cells lacking SABRE exhibit unregulated callose deposition and remodeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the callose staining data in Figure 8

claim: In seed plants, callose begins to accumulate during the ring phragmoplast stage
source: In seed plants, callose begins to accumulate during the ring phragmoplast stage (Park et al., 2014; Samuels et al., 1995), coincident with the timing of SABRE and ER recruitment along the cell plate (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations and correlated with the current findings

claim: Without SABRE, the ER still accumulates at the cell plate but buckles in the middle of the cell in a fully expanded phragmoplast
source: Without SABRE, the ER still accumulates, but in a fully expanded phragmoplast, the ER parallel to the cell plate invariably buckles in the middle of the cell.
evidence: This is a finding from ER imaging during cell division

claim: In ∆sabre cells, delayed/unregulated callose deposition occurs
source: In ∆sabre cells, we observed delayed/unregulated callose deposition.
evidence: This is a finding from callose staining experiments

claim: Both actin and microtubules are retained at the expanded phragmoplast in ∆sabre cells, possibly to lend structural support to the nascent cell plate lacking uniform callose
source: Perhaps to lend structural support to the nascent cell plate lacking uniform callose, both actin and microtubules were retained at the expanded phragmoplast.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cytoskeleton imaging data

claim: The SABRE-decorated ER domains contribute to regulating callose deposition
source: Taken together our data suggest that the SABRE-decorated ER domains contribute to regulating callose deposition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on SABRE localization and callose deposition

claim: SABRE influences the directionality and persistence of polarized growth and nuclear migration by altering ER function, not the cytoskeleton
source: Beyond cell division, we found that SABRE influences the directionality and persistence of polarized growth and nuclear migration by altering ER function, not the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on SABRE localization, ER behavior, and cytoskeleton analysis

claim: SABRE co-localizes to regions of the ER and does not impact cytoskeleton localization or dynamics
source: Using a combination of confocal microscopy and VAEM, we discovered that SABRE co-localizes to regions of the ER and does not impact cytoskeleton localization or dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microscopy data

source: In contrast to Arabidopsis cells, protonemata do not have an organized cortical microtubule array or a microtubule-based preprophase band, suggesting that these differences could result from cell type variability.

claim: Kinesin-14 drives basal nuclear movements in P. patens
source: Microtubule motor proteins that mediate these nuclear movements during cell division have been identified in P. patens. Kinesin-14 drives basal movements (Yamada and Goshima, 2018), and kinesin-13 drives apical nuclear movement during prophase (Leong et al., 2020).

source: Microtubule motor proteins that mediate these nuclear movements during cell division have been identified in P. patens. Kinesin-14 drives basal movements (Yamada and Goshima, 2018), and kinesin-13 drives apical nuclear movement during prophase (Leong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

source: The ER accumulates just below the cell tip where both actin and microtubules drive and steer polarized growth, respectively in protonemata.

source: However, in ∆sabre, both the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons were not affected, suggesting that SABRE's impact on cell expansion is independent of the cytoskeleton.

claim: Protonemata with impaired COPII function exhibit aggregated ER and polarized growth defects
source: Of note, a recent study demonstrated that protonemata with impaired COPII function, which mediates ER to Golgi transport, exhibited aggregated ER and polarized growth defects (Chang et al., 2020), suggesting that SABRE's influence on the ER might alter ER secretory function.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation

claim: Delivery of the plasma membrane protein SNAP-TM-mCherry is unaffected in ∆sabre
source: We discovered that delivery of the plasma membrane protein SNAP-TM-mCherry, which was affected in COPII mutants (Chang et al., 2020), was unaffected in ∆sabre.
evidence: This is a finding from imaging SNAP-TM-mCherry during cell division

claim: SABRE is the putative plant hobbit homolog
source: In a surprising connection, a study in Drosophila discovered hobbit, a protein that the authors report is conserved broadly across eukaryotes (Neuman and Bashirullah, 2018). SABRE is the putative plant hobbit homolog albeit with significant sequence divergence.
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to a Drosophila study

claim: Hobbit localizes to the ER when overexpressed in Drosophila
source: Even with the vast evolutionary distance between flies and plants, hobbit localizes to the ER when overexpressed in Drosophila and hobbit mutants are stunted similar to sabre null mutants in both Arabidopsis and P. patens.
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to a Drosophila study

claim: Hobbit mutants in Drosophila are stunted similar to sabre null mutants in both Arabidopsis and P. patens
source: Even with the vast evolutionary distance between flies and plants, hobbit localizes to the ER when overexpressed in Drosophila and hobbit mutants are stunted similar to sabre null mutants in both Arabidopsis and P. patens.
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to a Drosophila study and the current findings

source: In Drosophila, mutants in hobbit accumulated proteins required for membrane fusion in endosomal compartments and were defective specifically in insulin secretion, manifesting in stunted growth.

source: Our results have revealed that the ER does not simply repopulate at the daughter plasma membranes during cell division.

source: Furthermore, the ER via SABRE ultimately impacts cell expansion and nuclear migration.

claim: FM4-64 labels endocytic membranes
source: To follow membrane and cell wall remodeling events occurring during cell division, we imaged cell division in the presence of the lipophilic dye, FM4-64, and the callose-specific dye, aniline blue. FM4-64 labels endocytic membranes (Aniento and Robinson, 2005; Jelínková et al., 2010; Klima and Foissner, 2008; Kutsuna and Hasezawa, 2002; Tse et al., 2004; Ueda et al., 2004; van Gisbergen et al., 2008), which are readily incorporated into the membrane surrounding the nascent cell plate early in cytokinesis as clathrin-mediated endocytosis is integral for remodeling the tubular membrane network during early phragmoplast formation (Dhonukshe et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

claim: FM4-64 labeling decreases once the phragmoplast has expanded across the entire mother cell
source: However, once the phragmoplast has expanded across the entire mother cell, FM4-64 labeling decreases, consistent with a transition to different membrane trafficking machinery employed specifically during cell plate maturation and membrane fusion (Drakakaki, 2015; Park et al., 2014; Smertenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

claim: Aniline blue fluorescence steadily increases following a characteristic decrease in FM4-64 staining in wild type cells
source: By imaging actively dividing wild type cells, we observed that aniline blue fluorescence steadily increased following a characteristic decrease in FM4-64 staining (Figure 8A, Figure 8, Video 13).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging with dyes supported by Figure 8A and Video 13

claim: Aniline blue only stains cell plates that have fully expanded
source: Notably, aniline blue only stained cell plates that had fully expanded, suggesting that during phragmoplast expansion, callose within the membranous tubular network is not accessible to aniline blue in the extracellular environment.
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging with dyes

claim: As FM4-64 levels diminish during cell plate maturation and fusion, aniline blue can access the callose
source: However, as FM4-64 levels diminished, which occurred during cell plate maturation and fusion of the cell plate membrane with the parental plasma membrane, aniline blue could access the callose, leading to the observed increase in staining (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging with dyes supported by Figure 8A

claim: The FM4-64 signal continues to decrease for an additional 10 min in ∆sabre cells before aniline blue begins to rise
source: ∆sabre cells that divided relatively normally (contained no brown material) exhibited a similar decrease in FM4-64 intensity (Figure 8B, solid lines). However, the FM4-64 signal continued to decrease for an additional 10 min, before aniline blue began to rise.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from live imaging with dyes supported by Figure 8B

claim: The rate of increase in aniline blue is significantly slower in ∆sabre cells
source: Further, the rate of increase in aniline blue was significantly slower in ∆sabre cells (Figure 4B, dashed lines), suggesting that it either took longer for aniline blue to diffuse into the cell plate or that callose was deposited later in ∆sabre cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from live imaging with dyes supported by Figure 8B

claim: SNAP-TM-mCherry does not accumulate on the nascent cell plate
source: In these lines, loss of GFP fluorescence from the nucleus signaled nuclear envelope break down and the onset of prometaphase. In contrast to FM4-64, SNAP-TM-mCherry did not accumulate on the nascent cell plate (Figure 6, Figure 8C, Video 11).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging supported by Figure 8C and Video 11

claim: SNAP-TM-mCherry appears at the cell plate 30 min after nuclear envelope break down
source: Instead, SNAP-TM-mCherry appeared at the cell plate 30 min after nuclear envelope break down, the timing of which coincides with the end of phragmoplast expansion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging supported by Figure 8C

claim: SNAP-TM-mCherry disappears from the plasma membrane adjacent to the cell plate at the same time it appears at the cell plate
source: At the same time, SNAP-TM-mCherry disappeared from the plasma membrane adjacent to the cell plate (Figure 8C, white arrowheads), suggesting that SNAP-TM-mCherry accumulates at the cell plate by diffusing into the cell plate membrane from the parental plasma membrane once membrane fusion has occurred, rather than by delivery to the cell plate via exocytosis.
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging supported by Figure 8C with an interpretation

claim: ∆sabre cells exhibit the same SNAP-TM-mCherry kinetics as wild type
source: Interestingly ∆sabre cells exhibited the same SNAP-TM-mCherry kinetics as wild type, suggesting that diffusion from the parental plasma membrane was not impaired and thus membrane fusion is unaffected in ∆sabre.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from live imaging with an interpretation

claim: Membrane fusion is unaffected in ∆sabre
source: Interestingly ∆sabre cells exhibited the same SNAP-TM-mCherry kinetics as wild type, suggesting that diffusion from the parental plasma membrane was not impaired and thus membrane fusion is unaffected in ∆sabre.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SNAP-TM-mCherry imaging data

source: We found that compared to normal cell plates, which exhibited donut-shaped callose enrichments (Figure 8E), cells with brown material could be grouped into three categories: 27% stained weakly with aniline blue, 20% had a partial aniline blue ring, and 53% had large chunks of aniline blue staining near the brown material (Figure 8F; N = 15 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from callose staining supported by Figure 8F
